extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and authors reporting observational (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) epidemiological studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and reporting observational epidemiological study methods and results (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional), focusing on transparency about statistical methods, handling of confounding, missing data, participant flow, descriptive data, and outcome reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12 (a). Describe all statistical methods, including those used to control for confounding.
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe all statistical methods, including those used to control for confounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single correct analysis; investigators should pre-determine analyses at least for primary objectives in a study protocol and clarify whether particular analyses were suggested by data inspection or were pre-specified. If groups are not similar, adjustment should be made by stratification or multivariable regression. The study design often determines the type of regression (e.g., Cox for cohorts, logistic for case-control). Analysts should fully describe procedures for variable selection and not only present final model results; if model comparisons were used to select confounders, describe that process. Report if one or two covariates drive confounding. Describe other analyses (imputation, data transformation, attributable risks). Reference non-standard/novel approaches and report statistical software used. Describe methods “with enough detail to enable a knowledgeable reader with access to the original data to verify the reported results.” Also report how continuous and multi-category variables were entered into models and how confounders were chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12 (b). Describe any methods used to examine subgroups and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe any methods used to examine subgroups and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State which subgroup analyses were planned in advance and which arose during analysis. Explain methods used to examine whether effects differ across groups. Distinguish interaction (effect modification) on additive vs multiplicative scales; the additive scale (absolute risks) is generally more appropriate for public health and clinical decision-making. Present separate effects of both exposures and their joint effect (each relative to no exposure) and clearly state the analytic scale and methods (e.g., calculation of RERI and CIs). See item 17 for further discussion of subgroup analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box 5. Confounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators should think beforehand about potential confounding factors and how to address them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider confounders during design to inform data collection. Use restriction or matching where appropriate (matching may not always be desirable). In analysis, use stratification or multivariable analysis to reduce confounding. Stratification divides data into strata and combines estimates; multivariable analysis permits multiple variables simultaneously but may involve additional assumptions about functional form. Take confounders into account, but note adjusted analyses do not necessarily establish causality — residual confounding, random error, selection bias, and information bias may still distort results.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12 (c). Explain how missing data were addressed.
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how missing data were addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the number of missing values for each variable of interest and for each step in the analysis; give reasons for missing values if possible and indicate how many individuals were excluded because of missing data (see item 13 flow). Describe the nature of any analysis that accounts for missing data (e.g., multiple imputation) and the assumptions made (e.g., MAR). Authors should report methods used (e.g., MICE), number of imputed datasets, how estimates were pooled (e.g., Rubin's rules), and any software used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box 6. Missing data: problems and possible solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterise missing data (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and describe methods to handle them and their strengths/limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common approaches: complete-case analyses (can be unbiased but inefficient or biased if missingness related to outcomes), last observation carried forward (can distort trends), inserting missing-category indicators (may increase residual confounding), and imputation. Rubin's taxonomy: MCAR (missing independent of observed/unobserved), MAR (missing independent of unobserved values given observed), MNAR (missing depends on unobserved values). Methods for MAR: likelihood-based approaches, weighted estimation, and multiple imputation (most commonly used and flexible). Compare results with complete-case analyses and discuss important differences. Plausibility of assumptions is unverifiable; missing-data analyses are best viewed as sensitivity analyses (see items 12e and 17).

rubrics_metrics.name: 12 (d). Cohort study: If applicable, describe how loss to follow-up was addressed.
rubrics_metrics.description: For cohort studies, describe how loss to follow-up was addressed and what censoring strategies were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish persons who reach study end from those lost to follow-up; statistical software may not make this distinction. Decide at planning stage how to handle loss to follow-up. When few patients lost, options include excluding incomplete follow-up or treating them as withdrawn alive at date of loss or end of study. Report how many patients were lost and the censoring strategies used. Explain potential for informative censoring and its effect on validity; provide justification for excluding datasets/programs if inappropriate follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12 (d). Case-control study: If applicable, explain how matching of cases and controls was addressed.
rubrics_metrics.description: In matched case-control studies, explain how matching was accounted for in the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A crude analysis ignoring matching usually biases the estimate toward unity; matched analysis is often necessary. Matching can be viewed as stratified analysis: each case and its matched controls form a stratum. Methods include Mantel-Haenszel on matched 2x2 tables and conditional logistic regression (necessary when number of controls varies among cases or when adjusting for additional variables). Describe in detail the statistical methods used to analyse matched data. If taking matching into account has little effect, authors may present an unmatched analysis but should explain this choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12 (d). Cross-sectional study: If applicable, describe analytical methods taking account of sampling strategy.
rubrics_metrics.description: For cross-sectional studies, describe analytical methods that account for the sampling strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many cross-sectional studies use complex sampling (multi-stage, clustering, stratification, disproportionate sampling). State the method used to adjust for complex sampling so readers understand how sampling influenced precision (e.g., Taylor expansion method). Report measures like the design effect to show how precision differs from simple random sampling; with clustered sampling report design effects to make trade-offs transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12 (e). Describe any sensitivity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity analyses assess whether main results are consistent under alternative analysis strategies or assumptions. Examine issues including criteria for inclusion, definitions of exposures/outcomes, which confounders to adjust for, handling of missing data, possible selection bias, measurement error, and specific analysis choices (e.g., treatment of quantitative variables). Use sophisticated methods to model multiple biases simultaneously when appropriate. Sensitivity analyses can identify the degree of bias needed to explain an observed association or to assess robustness of null findings. Provide rationale and scenarios (e.g., extreme-case scenarios) and report results.

rubrics_metrics.name: RESULTS section: factual account without interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Results section should give a factual account of what was found and be free of interpretations and discursive text reflecting the authors' views and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include recruitment, description of study population, main results, and ancillary analyses. Avoid interpretive language in Results; reserve discussion of implications and interpretation for the Discussion section.

rubrics_metrics.name: 13 (a). Participants: Report numbers at each stage of the study
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the numbers of individuals at each stage—e.g., numbers potentially eligible, examined for eligibility, confirmed eligible, included in the study, completing follow-up, and analysed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed information on recruitment stages because included participants may differ from the target population and introduce response bias. Give counts at each stage appropriate to study type; for multistage sampling list numbers for different sampling units. In case-control studies, report flow separately for cases and controls and separately for controls recruited from different sources when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: 13 (b). Give reasons for non-participation at each stage.
rubrics_metrics.description: Give reasons for non-participation at each stage of recruitment and follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain reasons to help readers judge representativeness and potential for bias. Distinguish between non-participation unrelated to health (affects precision) and non-participation related to health status (can bias prevalence/incidence). Provide percentages and categorize reasons when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: 13 (c). Consider use of a flow diagram.
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider use of a flow diagram to present participant flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-structured flow diagram can convey recruitment and follow-up information transparently and may include main results (e.g., number of events for primary outcome). Recommended particularly for complex observational studies; no specific format prescribed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14 (a). Descriptive data: Give characteristics of study participants and information on exposures and potential confounders.
rubrics_metrics.description: Give characteristics of study participants (demographic, clinical, social) and information on exposures and potential confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize continuous variables by mean and SD or median and percentiles for skewed data. Do not present small-number ordered categories as continuous—give numbers and proportions for each category. In comparative studies, present descriptive characteristics and counts by group. Avoid inferential measures (SE, CIs) to describe variability in descriptive tables and avoid significance tests and P values for selecting confounders. For cohort studies, present how exposure relates to other characteristics; for case-control studies, explore source population of cases and describe controls appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14 (b). Indicate the number of participants with missing data for each variable of interest.
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate the number of participants with missing data for each variable of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because missing data may bias results or affect generalisability, report amounts of missing data for exposures, potential confounders, and other key variables. Use tables and figures to enumerate missing data and link to items 12c/Box 6 and extent of loss to follow-up (items 12d and 13).

rubrics_metrics.name: 14 (c). Cohort study: Summarise follow-up time—e.g., average and total amount.
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarise follow-up time in cohort studies (mean, median, total person-years, minimum, maximum, percentiles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report duration and extent of follow-up so readers can judge available outcome data. Present mean or median follow-up and/or total person-years, and optionally percentiles or min/max to show spread. Present such information separately for exposure categories when relevant. This allows calculation of event rates and transparency about captured potential data.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15 Outcome data (cohort): Report numbers of outcome events or summary measures over time.
rubrics_metrics.description: For cohort studies, report numbers of outcome events or summary measures over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report numbers of events for each outcome and consider reporting event rate per person-year. If risk changes over follow-up, present numbers and rates in appropriate follow-up intervals or present Kaplan–Meier life tables or plots. Consider cumulative incidence plots that start at 0% (preferable when event rate is low). Present such information separately by exposure categories of interest and for time-related quantitative outcomes present appropriate summaries over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15 Outcome data (case-control): Report numbers in each exposure category or summary measures of exposure.
rubrics_metrics.description: For case-control studies, report numbers in each exposure category or provide summary measures of exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on reporting exposures separately for cases and controls as frequencies or quantitative summaries to allow assessment of associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15 Outcome data (cross-sectional): Report numbers of outcome events or summary measures.
rubrics_metrics.description: For cross-sectional studies, report numbers of outcome events or appropriate summary measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present descriptive outcome data similarly to cohort studies but focusing on prevalence or summary measures appropriate to cross-sectional design.
